tool.name: csv
tool.tagline: Read and write CSV and other delimited files correctly in plain Python
tool.description: The csv module reads and writes comma-separated and other delimited text files, handling quoting, embedded commas and newlines, and spreadsheet dialects. It's the dependency-free way to import exports from Excel, databases and web services, or to produce files others can open. Knowing its rules avoids the corrupted-row bugs that come from splitting lines by hand.

glossary.def: In Python's csv module: a named set of formatting rules for a CSV file, such as which character separates values, which one quotes them and how lines end.
Tab-separated values: like CSV, but the values on each line are separated by tab characters instead of commas.
The csv module's reader that gives each row as a dict keyed by column name (DictWriter is its partner that writes such dicts).
A few invisible bytes that some programs, notably Excel, put at the very start of a text file to mark which encoding it uses, such as UTF-8.
An attack where a value in an exported CSV file starts with =, +, - or @, so a spreadsheet treats it as a formula and runs it when the file is opened.
Any object with the same methods as an open file (reading, writing, looping over lines), such as io.StringIO, so code written for files accepts it too.
A rule of thumb: a quick way of guessing that is usually right but can be wrong.
Request for Comments: a numbered document published by the internet's standards bodies. Many formats and protocols are written down in one, like CSV in RFC 4180.

concepts.name: Reading rows with csv.reader
concepts.summary: Open a CSV file with newline='' and loop over csv.reader to get each row as a list of strings.
concepts.why: CSV is the most common way to move tables of data between programs, and splitting lines on commas breaks on real data.
concepts.body:
A CSV file is a table saved as text. Each line is one **row**, such as one person, and commas split the row into **fields**: one value for each **column**. `Ada,London,36` is a row with three fields.

It looks simple, but a field may itself contain a comma, a quote mark or even a line break. Such a field is wrapped in double quotes, and a quote mark inside it is doubled: `"Smith, Jane","said ""hi"" twice"`. `line.split(",")` gets that wrong. `csv.reader` reads it correctly; working out the structure of text like this is called **parsing**.

```python
with open("people.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for row in csv.reader(f):
        print(row)
```

Each row comes back as a **list of strings**. Note the details:

- Open the file with `newline=""`. The csv module deals with line endings itself; without this, line breaks inside quoted fields can be changed and Windows-style `\r\n` line endings misread.
- Pass `encoding="utf-8"` (or whatever the file uses). Otherwise Python uses your computer's default, which differs between Windows and other systems.
- The reader hands out one row at a time as you loop, so even files bigger than your computer's memory are fine. You can only loop over it once.
- The header row (the column names) is just the first row. Take it out with `header = next(reader)`, which gets the next row.
- `reader.line_num` tells you which line of the file the reader has reached, useful in error messages.

Values are never converted: `"42"` stays a string. A blank line comes back as an empty list `[]`, so add `if not row: continue` when files may contain them.
concepts.code:
import csv

with open("people.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write('name,city,quote\nAda,London,"said ""hi"" twice"\n"Smith, Jane",Paris,"two\nlines"\n')

with open("people.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    reader = csv.reader(f)
    header = next(reader)
    print(header)                       # ['name', 'city', 'quote']
    for row in reader:
        print(reader.line_num, row)
# 2 ['Ada', 'London', 'said "hi" twice']
# 4 ['Smith, Jane', 'Paris', 'two\nlines']   (one row spread over two lines of the file)
takeaways: Always open CSV files with newline='' and an explicit encoding
csv.reader gives each row as a list of strings
Quoted fields may contain commas, quote marks and line breaks
pitfalls: Reading CSV with line.split(','), which breaks on quoted commas and line breaks.

quiz.q: Why does the csv documentation insist on open(..., newline='')?
options: So line breaks inside quoted fields and \r\n endings are handled by csv, not changed by Python
quiz.explain: csv handles line endings itself; if Python also changed them while reading, line breaks inside quoted fields would be altered.

concepts.name: Writing rows with csv.writer
concepts.summary: Write lists of values to a CSV file with csv.writer, letting it handle quoting automatically.
concepts.why: Hand-built CSV strings break as soon as a value contains a comma or quote; the writer never does.
concepts.body:
`csv.writer(f)` wraps a file opened for writing (again with `newline=""`). Then:

- `writer.writerow(["Ada", 36, "London, UK"])` writes one row,
- `writer.writerows(rows)` writes many rows at once, for example a list of lists.

The writer turns non-string values into text with `str()`, writes `None` as an empty field, and adds quotes only when needed. That's when a field contains the **delimiter** (the character that separates fields, normally the comma), a quote mark or a line break. Quote marks inside a field are doubled.

Lines end with `\r\n` by default, which is what Excel and the common CSV standard expect. That's why `newline=""` matters when writing too: on Windows, without it, Python would turn the `\n` into `\r\n` again, giving `\r\r\n` and blank rows between records in Excel.

Floats are written in full, so `0.1 + 0.2` becomes `0.30000000000000004` (a float can't store most decimal fractions exactly). Round or format numbers yourself if people will read the file: `f"{price:.2f}"`.

Use mode `"a"` to add rows to the end of an existing file, but only write the header row when the file is new.
concepts.code:
import csv

rows = [
    ["name", "age", "address", "note"],
    ["Ada", 36, "London, UK", 'says "hi" once'],
    ["Linus", None, "Helsinki", 0.1 + 0.2],
]
with open("out.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerows(rows)

print(repr(open("out.csv", newline="").read()))
# 'name,age,address,note\r\nAda,36,"London, UK","says ""hi"" once"\r\n'
# 'Linus,,Helsinki,0.30000000000000004\r\n'   (one string, shown split)
takeaways: csv.writer + writerow/writerows; open with newline=''
Quoting and doubling of quote marks happen automatically
None becomes an empty field; other values use str()
pitfalls: Opening the output file without newline='' on Windows, producing blank lines between rows.

quiz.q: What does csv.writer write for the value None?
quiz.explain: None is written as an empty string.

concepts.name: DictReader and DictWriter
concepts.summary: Work with rows as dictionaries keyed by column name using DictReader and DictWriter.
concepts.why: Accessing row['email'] instead of row[3] keeps code correct when columns are added or reordered.
concepts.body:
**csv.DictReader(f)** uses the first row as the column names and gives each following row as a `dict`: `row["email"]`. Since Python 3.8 these are plain dicts, in column order.

- `reader.fieldnames` gives the column names.
- Pass `fieldnames=[...]` if the file has no header row; then the first row is treated as data.
- If a row has more fields than there are column names, the extras go into a list under the key `restkey` (default `None`); missing fields get the value `restval` (default `None`).

**csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=[...])** writes dicts:

- `writer.writeheader()` writes the row of column names; call it once.
- `writer.writerow(d)` / `writerows(dicts)`: keys are matched to columns; missing keys get `restval` (default: an empty field).
- A dict with a key that isn't in `fieldnames` raises `ValueError`, unless you pass `extrasaction="ignore"`.

`fieldnames` also sets the order of columns in the output, so you can reorder or pick columns while copying a file. A typical script reads with DictReader, changes each dict, and writes it with DictWriter, one row at a time, so even huge files never need to fit in memory.
concepts.code:
import csv

with open("users.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["id", "email", "plan"])
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerow({"id": 1, "email": "ada@x.io", "plan": "pro"})
    w.writerow({"id": 2, "email": "bob@x.io"})              # plan -> ''

with open("users.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f, \
     open("emails.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as out:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    print(reader.fieldnames)                  # ['id', 'email', 'plan']
    writer = csv.DictWriter(out, fieldnames=["email", "id"], extrasaction="ignore")
    writer.writeheader()
    for row in reader:
        print(row)                            # {'id': '1', 'email': 'ada@x.io', 'plan': 'pro'} ...
        writer.writerow(row)                  # 'plan' ignored, columns reordered

print(open("emails.csv").read().split())      # ['email,id', 'ada@x.io,1', 'bob@x.io,2']
takeaways: DictReader gives one dict per row, keyed by the column names
DictWriter needs fieldnames and writeheader()
extrasaction='ignore' drops keys that aren't columns
pitfalls: Forgetting writeheader(), producing a file without column names.

quiz.q: DictWriter(f, fieldnames=['a']).writerow({'a': 1, 'b': 2}) is called. What happens?
options: Raises ValueError because b isn't a field
quiz.explain: The default extrasaction='raise' rejects unknown keys.

concepts.name: Converting types and missing values
concepts.summary: Turn CSV strings into ints, floats, dates and None, and know what QUOTE_NONNUMERIC does.
concepts.why: Every value from CSV is text; code that calculates needs real numbers and dates, and a rule for blanks.
concepts.body:
The csv module gives you strings only. Converting them is your job, and doing it in one place keeps the rest of the code clean:

```python
def parse(row):
    return {
        "id": int(row["id"]),
        "price": float(row["price"]) if row["price"] else None,
        "day": date.fromisoformat(row["day"]),
    }
```

Things to decide on purpose:

- **Empty strings**: does `""` mean missing (`None`), zero, or an error?
- **Number formats**: thousands separators (`"1,234"`), currency symbols and decimal commas (`"3,5"` in many European exports) need cleaning first. Use `decimal.Decimal` (exact decimal numbers) for money.
- **Booleans**: map `"yes"/"no"`, `"true"/"false"`, `"1"/"0"` yourself; `bool("false")` is `True`.
- **Dates**: `date.fromisoformat` for dates written like `2026-10-01`, `datetime.strptime` for any other layout.

`quoting=csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC` changes behaviour in both directions: the writer puts quotes around everything that isn't a number, and the reader turns every **unquoted** field into a `float`, raising `ValueError` if it can't. It only works for files written that way.

For heavy number crunching, the third-party libraries pandas and polars work out the types for you. The csv module is ideal when you want full control and nothing extra to install.
concepts.code:
import csv, io
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal

data = "sku,price,qty,day,active\nA1,19.99,3,2026-10-01,yes\nB2,,1,2026-10-02,no\n"

def parse(row):
    return {
        "sku": row["sku"],
        "price": Decimal(row["price"]) if row["price"] else None,
        "qty": int(row["qty"]),
        "day": date.fromisoformat(row["day"]),
        "active": row["active"].lower() in {"yes", "true", "1"},
    }

items = []
for r in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(data)):   # StringIO: a string used like a file
    items.append(parse(r))
print(items[0]["price"] * items[0]["qty"], items[1]["price"], items[1]["active"])
# 59.97 None False

buf = io.StringIO()
csv.writer(buf, quoting=csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC).writerow(["A1", 19.99, 3])
print(buf.getvalue().strip())                       # "A1",19.99,3
print(next(csv.reader(io.StringIO(buf.getvalue()), quoting=csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC)))
# ['A1', 19.99, 3.0]
takeaways: All fields are strings; convert them in one function
Decide what empty strings mean (None, 0, error)
QUOTE_NONNUMERIC makes the reader return floats for unquoted fields
pitfalls: Using bool(value) on CSV text; any non-empty string, including 'false', is True.

quiz.q: With quoting=csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC, what does the reader return for an unquoted field 3?
quiz.explain: Unquoted fields are converted to float.

concepts.name: Delimiters and dialects
concepts.summary: Read and write TSV and semicolon-separated files by setting delimiter, quotechar and lineterminator, or by naming a dialect.
concepts.why: Many exports aren't comma-separated at all: Excel in much of Europe uses semicolons, and many tools use tabs.
concepts.body:
"CSV" is really a family of formats. The csv module describes one as a **dialect**: a named set of formatting settings.

- `delimiter`: the field separator, default `","`. Use `"\t"` for **TSV** (tab-separated values), `";"` for many European spreadsheet exports, `"|"` for some database exports.
- `quotechar`: the quote character, default `'"'`.
- `lineterminator`: used by the **writer** only, default `"\r\n"`; the reader accepts `\r`, `\n` or `\r\n` whatever you set.
- `skipinitialspace=True`: ignore spaces after the delimiter, for files like `a, b, c`.
- `doublequote`, `escapechar`, `quoting`, `strict`: covered in the quoting lesson.

Pass settings directly, `csv.reader(f, delimiter=";")`, or name a dialect. The built-in ones are `"excel"` (the default), `"excel-tab"` and `"unix"` (which ends lines with `\n` and quotes all fields).

To reuse settings, register your own: `csv.register_dialect("pipes", delimiter="|", quoting=csv.QUOTE_NONE, escapechar="\\")`, then `csv.reader(f, dialect="pipes")`. `csv.list_dialects()` shows what's registered. Keyword arguments win over the dialect's values, so `dialect="excel", delimiter=";"` works.
concepts.code:
import csv, io

tsv = "name\tscore\nAda\t9.5\n"
print(list(csv.reader(io.StringIO(tsv), dialect="excel-tab")))
# [['name', 'score'], ['Ada', '9.5']]

euro = "name;price\nTea;3,50\n"
rows = list(csv.reader(io.StringIO(euro), delimiter=";"))
print(rows[1], float(rows[1][1].replace(",", ".")))  # ['Tea', '3,50'] 3.5

print(list(csv.reader(io.StringIO("a, b, c"), skipinitialspace=True)))  # [['a', 'b', 'c']]

csv.register_dialect("pipes", delimiter="|", lineterminator="\n")
buf = io.StringIO()
csv.writer(buf, dialect="pipes").writerows([["id", "msg"], [1, "a|b"]])
print(buf.getvalue(), end="")
# id|msg
# 1|"a|b"
print(csv.list_dialects())     # ['excel', 'excel-tab', 'unix', 'pipes']  (order may vary)
takeaways: delimiter, quotechar and lineterminator define the format
Built-in dialects: excel, excel-tab, unix
register_dialect names a reusable set of options
pitfalls: Setting lineterminator for the reader and expecting it to matter; it only affects writing.

quiz.q: Which call reads a semicolon-separated export correctly?
quiz.explain: delimiter is the field separator; the others control quoting, line ends and tabs.

concepts.name: Encodings and Excel
concepts.summary: Handle Excel's byte order marks, older encodings and Excel's quirks when reading and writing CSV.
concepts.why: Garbled column names and broken accents are the most common CSV problems people report.
concepts.body:
CSV files have no way to say which encoding they use, so you must know it or guess it.

**Reading**:
- Modern files are usually UTF-8. Files saved by Excel as "CSV UTF-8" start with a **byte order mark** (BOM): three invisible bytes that mark the file as UTF-8. Opened as `utf-8`, the first column name becomes `'\ufeffname'` and `row["name"]` raises `KeyError`. Use `encoding="utf-8-sig"`, which removes a BOM if there is one and works fine without one.
- Older Windows exports may use `cp1252`, an older Western European encoding; some systems produce `latin-1`. A `UnicodeDecodeError` (Python failing to turn the bytes into text) is a strong hint.
- `errors="replace"` keeps a script running on bad bytes by replacing them with `\ufffd` (the � symbol); print a warning when it happens.

**Writing for Excel**:
- Write with `encoding="utf-8-sig"` so Excel sees it's UTF-8. Without the BOM, Excel on Windows often assumes an older local encoding and shows accents as garbage.
- Excel in many European countries (it follows the computer's region settings) expects `;` between fields and `,` as the decimal separator.
- Excel interprets values: long numbers lose digits, leading zeros vanish, and `2-3` may become a date. That only changes what Excel shows; the file itself is fine.

**Security**: a field starting with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` may be run as a formula when the file is opened in a spreadsheet. This is called **CSV injection**: someone types a formula into a value that your program later exports. If users supply values for exports, put a `'` in front of such values, which tells the spreadsheet to treat them as text.
concepts.code:
import csv

with open("excel.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:   # writes BOM
    csv.writer(f).writerows([["name", "city"], ["José", "Zürich"]])

print(open("excel.csv", "rb").read()[:4])          # b'\xef\xbb\xbfn'  (BOM + 'n')

with open("excel.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(next(csv.DictReader(f)).keys())          # dict_keys(['\ufeffname', 'city'])

with open("excel.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
    print(next(csv.DictReader(f)))                 # {'name': 'José', 'city': 'Zürich'}

def safe_cell(value):
    return "'" + value if value[:1] in ("=", "+", "-", "@") else value
print(safe_cell("=HYPERLINK(\"http://evil\")"))   # '=HYPERLINK("http://evil")
takeaways: Read with utf-8-sig to strip an Excel BOM automatically
Write utf-8-sig when the file is meant for Excel
Neutralise leading = + - @ in user data to prevent CSV injection
pitfalls: Reading an Excel UTF-8 export with encoding='utf-8' and getting KeyError on the first column.

quiz.q: row['name'] raises KeyError although the header shows 'name'. The file came from Excel. Most likely fix?
quiz.explain: A BOM makes the first key '\ufeffname'; utf-8-sig strips it.

concepts.name: Quoting, escaping and embedded newlines
concepts.summary: Control quoting with the QUOTE_* constants, including QUOTE_STRINGS and QUOTE_NOTNULL, and use escapechar.
concepts.why: Swapping files with databases and strict CSV readers often requires a specific quoting style.
concepts.body:
The `quoting` setting controls when the writer puts quotes around fields, and how the reader treats quotes:

- `QUOTE_MINIMAL` (default): only fields containing special characters.
- `QUOTE_ALL`: every field.
- `QUOTE_NONNUMERIC`: everything that isn't a number; the reader turns unquoted fields into floats.
- `QUOTE_NONE`: never quote. The writer then needs an `escapechar` to mark delimiters inside fields, or it raises `csv.Error`.
- `QUOTE_STRINGS` (3.12+): quote all strings; `None` is written as an empty, unquoted field. The reader turns unquoted empty fields into `None` and other unquoted fields into floats.
- `QUOTE_NOTNULL` (3.12+): quote everything except `None`, which is written empty; the reader turns unquoted empty fields into `None`.

The last two finally let a CSV file keep `None` (`,,`) apart from an empty string (`,"",`) when you write it and read it back, a difference databases care about.

**Quote marks inside fields**: with `doublequote=True` (the default) a `"` is written as `""`. With `doublequote=False`, the writer puts the `escapechar` in front of it instead (`\"`).

**Line breaks inside fields** are allowed when the field is quoted: the reader returns one record spread over several lines of the file. Tools that work line by line, such as the `wc -l` line-counting command, `grep` or a simple split, miscount such files.
concepts.code:
import csv, io

def write(rows, **kw):
    buf = io.StringIO()
    csv.writer(buf, lineterminator="\n", **kw).writerows(rows)
    return buf.getvalue()

rows = [["id", "note", "score"], [1, "", None], [2, 'say "ok" now', 3.5]]
print(write(rows, quoting=csv.QUOTE_ALL), end="")
# "id","note","score" / "1","","" / "2","say ""ok"" now","3.5"
print(write(rows, quoting=csv.QUOTE_NOTNULL), end="")
# "id","note","score" / "1","", / "2","say ""ok"" now","3.5"
print(write([["a,b", 'q"']], quoting=csv.QUOTE_NONE, escapechar="\\"), end="")
# a\,b,q\"

back = csv.reader(io.StringIO('"x","",\n'), quoting=csv.QUOTE_NOTNULL)
print(next(back))                                    # ['x', '', None]
takeaways: QUOTE_MINIMAL, ALL, NONNUMERIC, NONE, STRINGS, NOTNULL control quoting
QUOTE_NOTNULL / QUOTE_STRINGS (3.12) tell None apart from empty strings
QUOTE_NONE needs an escapechar for special characters
pitfalls: Counting CSV records with wc -l when quoted fields contain newlines.

quiz.q: What distinguishes QUOTE_NOTNULL from QUOTE_ALL when writing None?
options: QUOTE_NOTNULL writes None as an empty unquoted field
quiz.explain: QUOTE_ALL writes "" for None; QUOTE_NOTNULL leaves it unquoted so readers can map it back to None.

concepts.name: Detecting formats with Sniffer
concepts.summary: Guess an unknown file's delimiter, quoting and header row with csv.Sniffer.
concepts.why: User uploads arrive as commas, semicolons or tabs, and you can't always ask which.
concepts.body:
`csv.Sniffer` looks at a sample of text and guesses the format.

- `Sniffer().sniff(sample, delimiters=None)` returns a dialect (a class holding the detected `delimiter`, `quotechar`, `doublequote` and `skipinitialspace`). Limit the candidates with `delimiters=",;\t|"` for more reliable results. It raises `csv.Error` ("Could not determine delimiter") when it can't decide.
- `Sniffer().has_header(sample)` guesses whether the first row is a header, using clues such as "the first row's values differ in type or length from the rest".

Typical use:

```python
sample = f.read(64 * 1024)
f.seek(0)
dialect = csv.Sniffer().sniff(sample, delimiters=",;\t")
reader = csv.reader(f, dialect)
```

Read a sample of a few kilobytes that ends near the end of a line, then go back to the start of the file with `seek(0)`.

These are **heuristics**: rules of thumb that are usually right but can be wrong. They fail on single-column files, tiny samples, or data where every column is text (then `has_header` can't tell a header from data). Use them for files users upload, with a fallback (default to `excel`) and ideally a preview the user can correct. For files you control, set the dialect explicitly instead.
concepts.code:
import csv, io

files = {
    "commas": "id,name,score\n1,Ada,9.5\n2,Bob,7.0\n",
    "semis":  "id;name;score\n1;Ada;9,5\n2;Bob;7,0\n",
    "tabs":   "1\tAda\t9.5\n2\tBob\t7.0\n",
}
sniffer = csv.Sniffer()
for label, text in files.items():
    d = sniffer.sniff(text, delimiters=",;\t")
    print(label, repr(d.delimiter), sniffer.has_header(text),
          next(csv.reader(io.StringIO(text), d)))
# commas ',' True ['id', 'name', 'score']
# semis ';' True ['id', 'name', 'score']
# tabs '\t' False ['1', 'Ada', '9.5']
try:
    sniffer.sniff("just one column\nno delimiters\n", delimiters=",;")
except csv.Error as e:
    print("csv.Error:", e)          # csv.Error: Could not determine delimiter
takeaways: Sniffer().sniff(sample) returns a dialect with the detected delimiter
has_header() guesses whether the first row is a header
Limit the delimiters and keep a fallback; sniffing is only a guess
pitfalls: Sniffing a sample and forgetting f.seek(0), so the reader starts mid-file.

quiz.q: What does Sniffer.sniff() raise when it can't decide on a delimiter?
quiz.explain: It raises csv.Error with 'Could not determine delimiter'.

concepts.name: Streaming, in-memory and large files
concepts.summary: Handle huge CSV files row by row with generators, and read or write CSV held in a string with io.StringIO.
concepts.why: Exports of millions of rows must not be loaded into memory at once, and web apps often build CSV files without saving them to disk.
concepts.body:
csv readers and writers work with any **file-like object** (anything with the methods of an open file) and handle one row at a time. That gives you two useful patterns.

**Streaming** means handling data piece by piece as it flows through. Chain generators so only one row is in memory at a time:

```python
def rows(path):
    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        yield from csv.DictReader(f)
big = (r for r in rows("events.csv") if r["type"] == "error")
writer.writerows(big)
```

`itertools.islice(reader, 10)` previews the first rows; `sum(1 for _ in reader)` counts records (not lines) without storing them. To insert rows into a database many at a time, group them into fixed-size **batches** with `itertools.batched(reader, 1000)` (3.12+).

**In memory**: `io.StringIO` is a file-like object that keeps its contents in a string. Read CSV that arrived as text, such as data downloaded from a web service or a file a user uploaded: `csv.reader(io.StringIO(text))`. To build a CSV file for a user to download, write into a `StringIO` and call `getvalue()`. For data that arrives as bytes, wrap it with `io.TextIOWrapper(binary, encoding="utf-8", newline="")`.

Writing to `sys.stdout` (the program's normal output) works too. That makes it easy to write command-line tools whose output feeds into other commands; pass `lineterminator="\n"` if you prefer Unix-style line endings.
concepts.code:
import csv, io, itertools

with open("events.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["id", "type"])
    w.writerows([i, "error" if i % 3 == 0 else "ok"] for i in range(1, 100_001))

def read_rows(path):
    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        yield from csv.DictReader(f)

errors = (r for r in read_rows("events.csv") if r["type"] == "error")
print([r["id"] for r in itertools.islice(errors, 3)])   # ['3', '6', '9']

batches = itertools.batched(read_rows("events.csv"), 40_000)
print([len(b) for b in batches])                        # [40000, 40000, 20000]

raw = io.BytesIO("name\nZoë\n".encode("utf-8"))       # e.g. an uploaded file
text = io.TextIOWrapper(raw, encoding="utf-8", newline="")
print(list(csv.reader(text)))                           # [['name'], ['Zoë']]
takeaways: Readers and writers work a row at a time; chain generators to keep memory use small
io.StringIO handles CSV text held in a string; TextIOWrapper adapts bytes
itertools.islice and batched help preview and group large files
pitfalls: Calling list(reader) on a multi-gigabyte file and running out of memory.

quiz.q: You downloaded CSV data from a web service and have it as one str. What's the simplest way to read it with csv.reader?
quiz.explain: StringIO wraps the string in a file-like object; passing the str directly would loop over single characters.

concepts.name: Malformed data and error handling
concepts.summary: Detect and report bad rows with strict mode, csv.Error, line numbers, field_size_limit and checks for rows of the wrong length.
concepts.why: Real-world files are messy; a robust import reports exactly which row failed and why, instead of crashing or silently mixing up data.
concepts.body:
The reader is forgiving by default: an unbalanced quote may silently swallow the rest of the file into one field, and a stray quote in the middle of a field is kept as text. Make problems visible:

- `strict=True` raises `csv.Error` on broken CSV, such as a character right after a closing quote.
- A file ending inside a quoted field raises `csv.Error: unexpected end of data` when `strict=True` is on.
- `reader.line_num` gives the line of the file where reading stopped, so error messages can point at it.
- `csv.field_size_limit()` (default 131072 characters) protects against a field that never ends; going over it raises `csv.Error: field larger than field limit`. Raise the limit on purpose with `csv.field_size_limit(n)` if you have big legitimate fields.

**Ragged rows** (rows with the wrong number of fields) are still valid CSV, so check them yourself: compare `len(row)` with the header, or use DictReader's `restkey` (extra values) and `restval` (missing values) to spot them.

A robust import keeps the jobs apart: csv reads the text, then your code checks each row's shape and types (**validation**), collects errors with line numbers instead of stopping at the first, and applies a policy: reject the whole file, skip bad rows, or set them aside in a separate file for a person to look at.
takeaways: strict=True turns broken quoting into csv.Error
reader.line_num locates problems; field_size_limit caps huge fields
Check field counts yourself; restkey/restval reveal ragged rows
pitfalls: Running a lenient reader over a file with an unbalanced quote, merging thousands of rows into one field.

quiz.q: Why can a single unbalanced quote be so damaging in non-strict mode?
options: Everything up to the next quote, including newlines, becomes one field
quiz.explain: The parser treats the following text, newlines included, as part of the quoted field.

concepts.name: CSV performance at scale
concepts.summary: Measure and speed up CSV processing: the C parser, per-row costs, reader vs DictReader, and when to switch tools.
concepts.why: Turning a 10-minute import into a 1-minute one usually takes a few simple changes.
concepts.body:
The `csv` module's parser is written in C (`_csv`), so reading the text itself is fast; most time goes into **your Python code that runs for every row**. Typical speedups:

- **`reader` over `DictReader`**: DictReader builds a dict for every row and is noticeably slower. In code that runs millions of times, read the header once, look up each column's position, and use plain lists.
- **Avoid repeated work** inside the loop: prepare **regular expressions** (text patterns) once before the loop, keep values you look up over and over in local variables, and convert only the columns you need.
- **Write in bulk**: `writer.writerows(generator)` beats calling `writerow` in a Python loop, and a bigger file **buffer** (`open(..., buffering=1 << 20)`) means Python goes to the operating system for data less often.

Beyond the parsing itself:

- **Group database work**: insert into a database many rows at a time (`executemany`), not one by one.
- **Use more CPU cores**: reading one file is sequential, but heavy per-row work can be split across several processes, a chunk of rows each.

Measure first with `time.perf_counter` or `cProfile`.

For number crunching or files of many gigabytes, tools that store and process data column by column are in another league: `pandas.read_csv`, `polars.read_csv`/`scan_csv` (uses several cores and reads only what a query needs) and DuckDB, which runs SQL queries on CSV files directly. Use the csv module for row-by-row changes, small-to-medium files and scripts with no extra installs; reach for those when you need totals and averages over hundreds of millions of rows.
takeaways: Parsing runs in fast C code; your per-row Python work dominates
Plain reader with column positions beats DictReader in code that runs for every row
Switch to pandas, polars or DuckDB for huge analysis jobs
pitfalls: Optimising the parser when the real cost is one database insert per row.

quiz.q: A CSV import is slow. What usually dominates the time?
options: Per-row Python work such as dict building, conversions and single-row inserts
quiz.explain: The parser is fast; the Python code run for each row is where time goes.

concepts.name: CSV semantics: RFC 4180 vs Python
concepts.summary: Know exactly how Python's csv relates to RFC 4180 and Excel: line endings, quoting rules, whitespace and empty lines.
concepts.why: Bugs when swapping files between programs come from small differences between what writers produce and what readers accept.
concepts.body:
There is no single official CSV standard. **RFC 4180** (2005), a published internet standards document, describes the common format: records separated by CRLF (the two characters `\r\n`), fields separated by commas, fields containing commas, quotes or line breaks wrapped in double quotes, and quote marks inside quoted fields doubled. An optional header line has the same format.

Python's default `excel` dialect matches it closely, but its reader deliberately accepts more:

- **Line endings**: the writer writes `\r\n`; the reader accepts `\r\n`, `\n` or `\r`. Inside quoted fields, line breaks are kept exactly, which only works if the file object doesn't change them, hence `newline=""`.
- **Spaces** count: `a, b` gives `' b'` unless `skipinitialspace=True`. RFC 4180 agrees: spaces are part of the field.
- **Empty lines** are returned as empty lists by `reader` and skipped by `DictReader`.
- **Quotes inside unquoted fields** (`ab"c`) are kept as they are in non-strict mode; RFC 4180 doesn't allow them.
- **The last line** may or may not end with a line break; both read the same.
- RFC 4180 says nothing about encoding (beyond naming the file type `text/csv` with an optional `charset`), types or missing values. That's why `QUOTE_NOTNULL` / `QUOTE_STRINGS` are Python conventions, not something other programs will understand.

When exchanging data, write down the dialect, encoding, header and how missing values are shown.
concepts.code:
import csv, io

cases = {
    "mixed endings": "a,b\r\nc,d\ne,f\rg,h",
    "spaces":        "a, b ,c",
    "blank lines":   "a\n\nb\n",
    "stray quote":   'ab"c,d',
    "quoted break":  '"line1\r\nline2",x',
}
for name, text in cases.items():
    print(f"{name:14}", list(csv.reader(io.StringIO(text, newline=""))))
# mixed endings  [['a', 'b'], ['c', 'd'], ['e', 'f'], ['g', 'h']]
# spaces         [['a', ' b ', 'c']]
# blank lines    [['a'], [], ['b']]
# stray quote    [['ab"c', 'd']]
# quoted break   [['line1\r\nline2', 'x']]
print(list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO("h\n\n1\n"))))    # [{'h': '1'}]  (blank skipped)
takeaways: Python's excel dialect closely follows RFC 4180, but its reader accepts more
Spaces are data; blank lines give [] in reader and are skipped by DictReader
Encoding, types and missing values are outside the standard: write them down
pitfalls: Assuming every program writes RFC 4180 CSV; check for stray quotes and spaces in hand-made files.

quiz.q: What does csv.reader return for the line 'a, b'?
quiz.explain: Whitespace after the delimiter is part of the field unless skipinitialspace=True.
